info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 4.2: Layout Analysis and HTR Model Training in Transkribus.

name.text: 01 Question: What "Deterministic" Means This Week

questiontext.text: In what sense is today's handwriting program "deterministic", given that it learns from examples rather than following written rules?

generalfeedback.text: A specialized HTR model is bounded by its training data, which makes it fail rather than fabricate — the opposite of Friday's tools.

answer.text: The same picture always gives the same answer, and it only knows what its examples taught it.

feedback.text: Correct. That boundary is a weakness and a protection at once — it will fail on unfamiliar writing, but it will not invent a convincing sentence.

answer.text: A person wrote out the rules for recognizing each Greek letter, so its behaviour is fully predictable.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Nobody wrote those rules; it learned the shapes from examples. The determinism is about repeatability and boundedness.

answer.text: It produces a different answer each time and averages them, which makes the result stable.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It does not vary between runs at all — that is part of what makes it deterministic.

answer.text: It can be made deterministic by turning off a randomness setting before each run.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no such switch in play here. The term describes the kind of system it is.

name.text: 02 Question: Finding the Lines Comes Before Reading Them

questiontext.text: The program reads most of a page well but produces gibberish on one part. Where should you look first?

generalfeedback.text: Recognition only ever sees line images that layout analysis produced — so when output is bad, inspect the line images first.

answer.text: At the strip of image cut out for that line, because the reading step never sees the page — only the strips.

feedback.text: Correct. If the strip is wrong, no amount of cleverness in the reading step can rescue it.

answer.text: At the base model, since gibberish means the script does not match what it was trained on.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A mismatched base model degrades the whole page evenly, not one patch of it.

answer.text: At your transcription, since gibberish means the training text contained errors there.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Worth checking eventually, but a localized failure points at how that area was cut up.

answer.text: At the number of training passes, since too few produces unstable output in places.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Undertraining affects everything, not one region.

name.text: 03 Question: Why Rectangles Do Not Work

questiontext.text: Why did line-finding move from drawing rectangles to following baselines?

generalfeedback.text: Modern layout analysis predicts sloping baselines and computes envelopes around them, because manuscript lines do not fit rectangles.

answer.text: A rectangle cannot describe a line that slopes or curves, and manuscript lines routinely do both.

feedback.text: Correct. A baseline can bend and follow the writing, and the strip is then worked out from it.

answer.text: Rectangles are slower to compute than baselines on large images.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are cheaper to compute. They are simply wrong for the shape of manuscript writing.

answer.text: Rectangles cannot be stored in ALTO or PAGE XML, which require baselines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both formats can hold either. The change was driven by accuracy, not by file formats.

answer.text: Baselines allow the program to read the line in both directions at once.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Direction of reading is unrelated. Baselines describe the line's actual course.

name.text: 04 Question: Loading Your Manuscript In

questiontext.text: Why import images by web address rather than uploading copies of the files?

generalfeedback.text: Import by manifest URI so training data stays linked to the institutional source rather than becoming a detached copy.

answer.text: The pictures stay the library's, served at their quality, so the trail from your training examples back to the original is unbroken.

feedback.text: Correct. You avoid making a private copy that quietly drifts out of date.

answer.text: Uploaded files are compressed by the platform and lose too much detail.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is not the reason given. The point is provenance — keeping the link to the institutional source.

answer.text: Transkribus has no facility for uploading files at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The argument is about why the address route is better, not about what is possible.

answer.text: Web addresses let several students share one collection without duplicating storage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Convenient perhaps, but not the reason. The reason is that the source stays authoritative.

name.text: 05 Question: Running It, Then Checking It

questiontext.text: You zoom in on a line with a high breathing mark and find it sits outside the strip boundary. What follows?

generalfeedback.text: Check whether polygons enclose high-placed breathings and accents — if they do not, the model is being trained on Greek with the diacritics cut off.

answer.text: Every accent in your training examples is being thrown away before the program ever sees it.

feedback.text: Correct. The model will then learn that Greek has no breathing marks, and reproduce that faithfully.

answer.text: The breathing mark will be read as belonging to the line above.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is not reassigned — it is simply absent from the image handed to the reading step.

answer.text: The program will automatically widen the strip when it detects a mark outside it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It does not know the mark is there. That is precisely why you have to check.

answer.text: Nothing follows, since accents are added separately after recognition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are read from the image like everything else.

name.text: 06 Question: Fixing the Lines by Hand

questiontext.text: What is the time-saving approach to correcting strips that cut off accents across many pages?

generalfeedback.text: Adjust the layout parameters from a measurement of this hand rather than correcting page by page — and verify by looking at extracted line images.

answer.text: Fix one page properly, measure how much room this hand needs, then change the line-finding settings and re-run the rest.

feedback.text: Correct. Changing one setting beats fixing fifty pages, and it treats the cause rather than the symptoms.

answer.text: Train a first model on the uncorrected pages and let it learn to compensate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It cannot compensate for marks that are not in the image it was given.

answer.text: Crop every page more generously before importing, so the strips have room.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Cropping the page does not change where the strip boundary is drawn around a line.

answer.text: Skip the affected lines and train on the ones whose strips are already correct.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That discards exactly the material with the high accents, which is what you need it to learn.

name.text: 07 Question: Matching Your Text to the Right Lines

questiontext.text: Your transcription has 24 lines; the program found 25, having split one. What happens if you let it match them up automatically?

generalfeedback.text: Verify line alignment by spot-checking image against text — an off-by-one misalignment produces a model that has learned the wrong pairing entirely.

answer.text: Every line after the split is paired with the wrong picture, teaching the program to match each line's image to the next line's words.

feedback.text: Correct. The output then reads smoothly and is entirely wrong, and the cause is very hard to spot afterwards.

answer.text: The extra line is left unpaired and simply ignored during training.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Matching proceeds in order, so everything after the split shifts by one.

answer.text: The platform refuses to proceed until the counts agree.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It will proceed, which is why the check is yours to make.

answer.text: The model trains normally but with slightly noisier data.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is not noise — it is a systematic, consistent mismatch, which is far worse.

name.text: 08 Question: How the Reading Step Works

questiontext.text: Why is your line-by-line transcription directly usable as training material, with no further annotation?

generalfeedback.text: CTC training needs only line images paired with line text, which is why your diplomatic transcription is directly usable as training data.

answer.text: The program does not need to be told which pixels belong to which letter — a strip of image paired with its text is enough.

feedback.text: Correct. It considers every possible way of lining the picture up with the letters and learns from all of them at once.

answer.text: Because you already marked each letter's position when you drew the zones in Lesson 3.3.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those zones are per line, not per letter — and the program does not use them for training.

answer.text: Because the program infers letter positions from the accents, which are evenly spaced.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Accent spacing plays no such role.

answer.text: Because TEI markup tells the program where each character begins and ends.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It never sees your TEI. It sees a strip and a string of text.

name.text: 09 Question: What Its Mistakes Look Like

questiontext.text: Why is it an advantage that this kind of program outputs `ἐγενθτο` rather than a real Greek word?

generalfeedback.text: A CTC model's errors are conspicuous because it produces impossible sequences rather than plausible wrong words — which makes post-correction far more reliable.

answer.text: An impossible string of letters announces itself, so you spot the error instantly when correcting.

feedback.text: Correct. A program that outputs a perfectly good word which is simply not on the page is far more dangerous.

answer.text: Because impossible strings are automatically flagged by the platform for review.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Nothing flags them. They are conspicuous to *you*, which is the point.

answer.text: Because impossible strings indicate the line strip was cut incorrectly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They usually indicate genuinely unclear ink. Gibberish across a whole line is the layout signal.

answer.text: Because they can be corrected automatically by a spellchecker.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Correcting toward plausible words is exactly the behaviour the course warns against.

name.text: 10 Question: The Newer Kind of Model

questiontext.text: TrOCR uses context to interpret unclear ink. Why is that both an advantage and a liability?

generalfeedback.text: Transformers read context as well as ink, which helps on degraded text and produces plausible wrong words that are hard to catch.

answer.text: It reads damaged pages better, and it is pulled toward whatever word is likely, so it hands you believable readings that do not match the ink.

feedback.text: Correct. The same mechanism produces both effects, which is why you must check its output far more carefully.

answer.text: It is faster but needs far more training examples than a simpler model.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Speed and data volume are not the trade-off described here — the trade-off is between context and invention.

answer.text: It reads accents better but loses the letters underneath them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no such trade. The issue is invented words, not lost marks.

answer.text: It works well on Greek but poorly on Latin scripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The difference is not between scripts but between reading ink and predicting language.

name.text: 11 Question: Never Start From Nothing

questiontext.text: Perdiki and Konstantinidou trained on identical mixed-manuscript material two ways. What did they find?

generalfeedback.text: Transfer learning turned 17.18% CER into 3.90% on identical data — always fine-tune from a base model rather than training from scratch.

answer.text: From nothing, 17.18% of characters wrong; starting from an existing model, 3.90%.

feedback.text: Correct. Four times better, from the single decision to start from a trained base rather than from scratch.

answer.text: From nothing, 3.90%; starting from an existing model, 17.18%, because the base model's habits interfered.

feedback.text: Incorrect — the figures are the other way round. Starting from an existing model helped enormously.

answer.text: Both approaches converged on about 8% once training ran long enough.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They did not converge; the gap was fourfold and persisted.

answer.text: Starting from an existing model was faster but slightly less accurate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It was both faster and dramatically more accurate.

name.text: 12 Question: Picking What to Start From

questiontext.text: Which matters most when choosing the model you start from, and why?

generalfeedback.text: A matched small model beats a large general one — script match matters more than parameter count.

answer.text: The script — a model trained on Latin handwriting has learned Latin letters and will not help with Greek, however large it is.

feedback.text: Correct. Bigger is not better; matched is better. Date and language come next, because they set the vocabulary and short forms.

answer.text: The number of settings inside the model, since larger models generalize better.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is the counter-intuitive part: a small matched model beat large general ones by a wide margin.

answer.text: How recently the model was published, since newer models supersede older ones.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Recency is no guide at all. A recent general model performed far worse than an older specialist.

answer.text: Whether the model is free, since paid models cannot be cited in a scholarly edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Cost bears on reproducibility, which is a separate matter discussed later.

name.text: 13 Question: Training the Model

questiontext.text: What are the held-back lines for, and what does it mean if the error on them starts rising?

generalfeedback.text: Hold out a representative validation set and stop when validation error stops falling — a rising validation curve means the model is memorizing your lines.

answer.text: They test whether the program learned the handwriting or merely memorized your lines; a rising error means it has begun memorizing.

feedback.text: Correct. Stop at the lowest point — training further makes it worse on anything it has not already seen.

answer.text: They are extra training material added at the end to improve the final score.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They must never be trained on, or they cannot test anything.

answer.text: They measure how fast the program runs, and a rising figure means it is running out of memory.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The figure is an error rate, not a speed or a memory measure.

answer.text: A rising error means the base model was mismatched and training should restart.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That would show as poor results throughout, not as a curve that falls and then rises.

name.text: 14 Question: Reading the Score

questiontext.text: Your model scores 18% of characters wrong. What should you do?

generalfeedback.text: Above 15% CER, correcting the output costs more than transcribing from scratch — the model is a net loss, not a slow tool.

answer.text: Diagnose rather than correct — past roughly 15%, fixing the output takes longer than typing the page from scratch.

feedback.text: Correct. Check line-finding, then alignment, then how much training material, then the starting model.

answer.text: Correct the output anyway, since any machine help is faster than typing from nothing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Above that threshold it is a net loss, not a slow tool.

answer.text: Accept it, since under 20% is regarded as usable for bulk corpus work.

feedback.text: Incorrect. 5–10% is good and 10–15% is borderline. 18% is poor.

answer.text: Train for more passes, since a high score always means undertraining.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Undertraining is one possibility among several, and not the first to check.

name.text: 15 Question: The Score Does Not Tell You Everything

questiontext.text: Why might a model scoring 8% be more useful to a scholar than one scoring 4%?

generalfeedback.text: CER weights every difference equally, so a model that silently drops diacritics or expands abbreviations can score well while being useless for a diplomatic edition.

answer.text: Because the 4% model may be quietly spelling out short forms — clean, readable, and destroying what the transcription exists to preserve.

feedback.text: Correct. The score treats every difference as equal, though what they cost a scholar differs enormously.

answer.text: Because a higher score means the model is being more careful with difficult passages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A higher score simply means more characters wrong. The argument is about *which* characters.

answer.text: Because 8% models run faster and use less computing time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Speed is not the issue here.

answer.text: Because scores below 5% are considered unreliable and are usually measurement errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Under 5% is excellent, and genuine. The caution is about what the number conceals.

name.text: 16 Question: Running the Model and Looking at What Comes Back

questiontext.text: Why sort the mistakes into categories rather than simply correcting them as you go?

generalfeedback.text: Categorize errors rather than just correcting them, and inspect the line image whenever output is nonsense — it is usually a layout fault.

answer.text: The sorted counts are a required part of the Week 5 report, and they are far easier to produce now than to reconstruct later.

feedback.text: Correct. Categories also reveal whether mistakes bunch by region, by letter, or by feature — which tells you the cause.

answer.text: Because correcting them now would invalidate the raw output for scoring.

feedback.text: Incorrect — but only if you correct before committing. Commit the raw output first, then correct freely.

answer.text: Because the platform can retrain automatically from categorized errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It retrains from corrected text, not from your categories.

answer.text: Because uncategorized corrections cannot be committed to git.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They can. The reason is analytical, not technical.

name.text: 17 Question: Going Round Again

questiontext.text: What is the feedback trap in the correct-and-retrain loop, and how do you break it?

generalfeedback.text: Each iteration makes ground truth cheaper, but correcting model output risks a feedback loop — periodically transcribe a page blind to break it.

answer.text: Careless corrections get learned and reproduced, then look familiar and are corrected even less carefully — so type a page from scratch occasionally and compare.

feedback.text: Correct. The loop can otherwise settle on a model that is confidently wrong.

answer.text: The model forgets earlier pages as new ones are added, so keep the training set small.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Adding material generally helps. The danger is the quality of what you add.

answer.text: Each round takes longer than the last, so stop after three iterations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Each round takes *less* effort per page — that is what makes the method worthwhile.

answer.text: The score improves on held-back lines but worsens on training lines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is backwards, and describes nothing that happens here.

name.text: 18 Question: Models Are Fragile About Layout

questiontext.text: Geelhaar's model scored 5.1% on ordinary pages and 13.6% on glossed ones, with the same scribe and language. What does that teach you?

generalfeedback.text: A model's CER holds only for layouts like those it was validated on — glossed or irregular pages need their own measurement.

answer.text: A score describes a layout, so pages laid out differently need measuring separately.

feedback.text: Correct. Smaller writing, different vocabulary, and heavier short forms were enough to take it from excellent to borderline.

answer.text: That marginal notes are usually written by a different scribe.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The scribe and language were identical. Layout alone accounted for it.

answer.text: That the model had been undertrained and needed more passes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It performed excellently on standard pages — it was not undertrained.

answer.text: That glossed pages should always be excluded from an edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They should be measured separately and, for training, deliberately included.

name.text: 19 Question: Transkribus and eScriptorium

questiontext.text: What does an open platform offer that a commercial one does not, for a scholarly edition?

generalfeedback.text: Transkribus is more accessible; eScriptorium is reproducible — and a proprietary model makes any claim resting on it unverifiable later.

answer.text: A model others can inspect and re-run, so a later scholar can verify your result.

feedback.text: Correct. A secret model might not exist in ten years, and any claim resting on it then becomes impossible to check.

answer.text: Better accuracy, since open models are trained on more material.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Accuracy is not the distinction. Transkribus has the larger ready-made library.

answer.text: A friendlier interface, which is why it is recommended for beginners.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The opposite — ease of use is the commercial platform's advantage, and it matters.

answer.text: Free credits for training, which commercial platforms charge for.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Costs differ, but the argument here is about whether your work can be checked.

name.text: 20 Question: Getting the Text Back Out

questiontext.text: How do the three line boxes you measured by hand in Lesson 3.3 earn their keep today?

generalfeedback.text: ALTO preserves line coordinates in image pixels — transform them into TEI zones and check the result against your hand-measured control lines.

answer.text: They are a known-good control: convert the exported coordinates and compare, and a consistent discrepancy reveals a scaling error.

feedback.text: Correct. Exported coordinates are in image pixels, so they need scaling if the viewer's canvas size differs.

answer.text: They are added to the export to fill in lines the program failed to detect.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are a check on the conversion, not a supplement to the output.

answer.text: They tell the platform what size to make the line strips.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Strip size comes from the baseline and the settings, not from your TEI.

answer.text: They are required by ALTO, which cannot record coordinates without a reference box.

feedback.text: Incorrect. ALTO records coordinates directly. The control is yours, for verification.

name.text: 21 Question: Saving Machine Output to Git

questiontext.text: Why must the raw output be committed separately, before you correct anything?

generalfeedback.text: Commit raw model output and your corrections separately, or Week 5 cannot compute an error rate at all.

answer.text: The raw output is what gets scored in Week 5 — commit it already corrected and there is nothing left to score.

feedback.text: Correct. It is not neatness; it is what makes the measurement possible at all.

answer.text: Because corrections must be reviewed by another student before being committed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No such review step exists.

answer.text: Because git cannot record two kinds of change in one commit.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It can. The separation is required by the methodology, not by the tool.

answer.text: Because the labels only apply to commits containing no human edits.

feedback.text: Incorrect — that is a consequence of the rule, not its reason. The reason is that the raw state must survive.

name.text: 22 Question: Setting Friday Up

questiontext.text: Why record the time you spent today, as well as the score?

generalfeedback.text: Record cost as well as quality — Friday's tool needs no training or ground truth, and the comparison is meaningless without that.

answer.text: Friday's tool needs no training, no line-fixing, and no examples, so comparing quality without comparing cost misses half the question.

feedback.text: Correct. The honest Week 5 assessment needs both figures.

answer.text: Because the time spent is part of the mark for the Transcription Assignment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It feeds the report's argument, not a time-based mark.

answer.text: Because Transkribus bills credits by the hour and you must report usage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Credits are consumed by training runs, and that is not why the time is recorded.

answer.text: Because slower training indicates a mismatched base model.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The timing being recorded is your effort, not the machine's.

name.text: 23 Question: Why the Small Specialist Usually Wins

questiontext.text: GPT-4o gets 1.39% wrong on modern English handwriting and 52.23% on historical English. What does the gap show?

generalfeedback.text: General models are excellent on modern handwriting and catastrophic on historical scripts — scale does not substitute for exposure to the material.

answer.text: Sheer size does not substitute for having been shown the actual material — the internet holds very little old handwriting.

feedback.text: Correct. Same model, same language; only the century changed.

answer.text: That historical English is a fundamentally harder language than modern English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is the same language. What differs is how well represented the handwriting is.

answer.text: That the historical test set was too small to give a reliable figure.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Nothing suggests that, and the pattern repeats across several datasets and models.

answer.text: That the model needs a larger image resolution for historical documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Resolution is not what accounts for a fortyfold difference.

name.text: 24 Question: More Steps Can Make It Worse

questiontext.text: Why does adding an AI step to tidy up reading output make the result worse rather than better?

generalfeedback.text: Adding LLM post-correction to OCR degrades quality — it corrects toward plausibility, and unusual readings are the interesting ones.

answer.text: The tidying step cannot see the picture, so it corrects toward whatever sounds likely — and unusual readings are often the interesting ones.

feedback.text: Correct. Anything broken late in the chain has nothing after it to catch the problem.

answer.text: Because the extra step doubles the processing time for no gain.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The cost is quality, not time.

answer.text: Because the two programs use incompatible character encodings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Encoding is not the issue — the issue is correcting toward plausibility without seeing the source.

answer.text: Because the tidying step overwrites the raw output, so nothing can be measured.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You can keep both. The finding is that the tidied text is genuinely worse.

name.text: 25 Question: Checklist Before You Leave

questiontext.text: In what order should you diagnose a model that scored worse than 15%?

generalfeedback.text: If validation CER exceeds 15%, diagnose rather than correct — check layout, then alignment, then data volume, then base model.

answer.text: Line-finding, then alignment, then how much training material, then the starting model.

feedback.text: Correct. Most first models are fixable, and the order runs from the most likely cause to the least.

answer.text: Starting model, then training passes, then image resolution, then alignment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The starting model is checked last, not first — line-finding faults are far more common.

answer.text: Retrain immediately with more passes before investigating anything.

feedback.text: Incorrect. More passes will not fix bad strips or mismatched text, and it spends shared credits.

answer.text: Correct the output first, then retrain on the corrections.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Above 15% the output is not worth correcting — that is the whole point of the threshold.

name.text: 26 Question: Things That Go Wrong Today

questiontext.text: The output is fluent and reads coherently, but it does not match the page. What is the likely cause?

generalfeedback.text: When output is inexplicably wrong, look at the extracted line image — that is what the model actually saw.

answer.text: Your transcription was attached one line out, so the model learned each line's picture with the next line's words.

feedback.text: Correct. The text is internally coherent and simply belongs somewhere else — spot-check picture against words to confirm.

answer.text: The strips were cut too tightly, removing the accents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That produces text missing its accents, not coherent text belonging elsewhere.

answer.text: The base model was trained on tidied text and is spelling short forms out.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That shows as expanded abbreviations, not as wholesale displacement.

answer.text: The model overfitted and is reproducing memorized training lines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Memorized lines would match the page they came from. Here the pairing itself is wrong.

name.text: 27 Question: Writing Down What You Did

questiontext.text: Why is a score of 6.2% meaningless on its own?

generalfeedback.text: A CER figure is uninterpretable without its base model, training volume, and validation set — record the methodology today.

answer.text: Without the starting model, the amount of training material, and what was in the held-back set, nobody can tell what it measures.

feedback.text: Correct. Record it now — if Week 5's results surprise you, this is what lets you work out why.

answer.text: Because scores must always be reported alongside a word-level figure as well.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A word-level figure helps, but it is not what makes the character figure interpretable.

answer.text: Because 6.2% is within the margin of error for any small test set.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Nothing in the lesson suggests that. The problem is missing context, not statistical noise.

answer.text: Because scores are only comparable between students using the same manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are not comparable between manuscripts, but that is not why the methodology is recorded.

name.text: 28 Question: Preparing for Friday

questiontext.text: Why must all three versions be saved under tags before Friday?

generalfeedback.text: Tag all three states so Friday's three-way comparison is exact, and expect the general model to be much worse and much faster.

answer.text: Friday compares your typing, today's model, and the general AI on the same lines, and tags make that comparison exact rather than approximate.

feedback.text: Correct. A tag is a permanent name for one particular version, retrievable from anywhere.

answer.text: Because tagged versions are the only ones that can be pushed from off campus.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Any commit can be pushed. Tags do need pushing explicitly, which is a separate trap.

answer.text: Because the AI model reads the tags to know which version to compare against.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It reads a picture. The tags are for you and for Week 5.

answer.text: Because untagged work is not eligible for the Transcription Assignment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The requirement is methodological — exact retrieval of the state that was measured.

name.text: 29 Question: What Good Work Looks Like Here

questiontext.text: What turns today's work from button-pushing into scholarship?

generalfeedback.text: Reporting *what* the model gets wrong and why is the scholarly contribution; the CER number alone is tool operation.

answer.text: Saying what the model gets wrong and why — which letterform, which short form, which kind of page.

feedback.text: Correct. That tells you what to fix, what to check by hand, and whether the method suits this manuscript. A bare score does none of it.

answer.text: Reaching a score below 5%, which is the threshold for a publishable model.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no such threshold, and a low score can conceal serious damage.

answer.text: Training several models and reporting the best score achieved.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Reporting only the best run hides more than it shows.

answer.text: Using the largest available base model, to rule out undertraining.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Larger is not better here — matched is better.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: An Instrument with Edges

questiontext.text: What does it mean to call a trained reading model "an instrument with edges"?

generalfeedback.text: An HTR model reads ink within the bounds of its training and fails conspicuously; Friday's instrument reads expectation too, and fails fluently.

answer.text: It reads ink and produces letters, and its competence extends exactly as far as its examples went — no further, and it does not pretend otherwise.

feedback.text: Correct. Inside that boundary it is fast, cheap, consistent, and inclined to fail loudly rather than to invent.

answer.text: It works only on rectangular pages with clearly ruled margins.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The edges are the limits of its training, not a physical constraint on the page.

answer.text: It has a fixed maximum accuracy that no amount of training can exceed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Accuracy improves with better data. The boundary is about what material it can handle.

answer.text: It must be retrained from scratch whenever the manuscript changes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You fine-tune it further — starting from scratch is precisely what you should never do.
